关键词: U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven T. Mnuchin
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Mick Mulvaney
主要内容: On October 15, 2018, U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven T. Mnuchin and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Mick Mulvaney released details of the fiscal year (FY) 2018 budget results. The FY 2018 deficit was $779 billion, $113 billion higher than the previous year but $70 billion less than the FY 2019 Mid-Session Review (MSR) forecast. As a percentage of GDP, the deficit was 3.9%, up from 3.5% in FY 2017. The administration attributed the economic growth to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) and a renewed focus on economic freedom, citing record job growth, increased consumer confidence, and a 2.9% real GDP growth over the past four quarters. The FY 2018 deficit was $54 billion less than the FY 2019 Budget estimate and $70 billion less than the MSR estimate. The administration emphasized the need for fiscal restraint and proposed measures to reduce the deficit by $3.6 trillion over 10 years. Total government receipts for FY 2018 amounted to $3,329 billion, an increase of $14 billion compared to FY 2017, representing a 0.4 percent rise. This was $6.8 billion above the Mid-Session Review (MSR) estimate. Receipts as a percentage of GDP were 16.5 percent, lower than the 17.2 percent in FY 2017 and below the 40-year average. The increase in receipts was primarily due to higher net individual income tax receipts, excise taxes, social insurance and retirement receipts, and customs duties, partially offset by lower net corporation income tax receipts and other factors. Outlays for FY 2018 totaled $4,108 billion, a 3.2 percent increase from FY 2017, with outlays as a percentage of GDP at 20.3 percent, slightly lower than the previous year and the 40-year average of 20.6 percent. The increase in outlays was attributed to higher spending on defense, Medicaid, Social Security, disaster relief, and other programs. Total Federal borrowing from the public increased by $1,084 billion to $15,751 billion, with borrowing as a percentage of GDP rising from 76.1 percent to 78.0 percent. The report highlighted several key areas where actual spending and receipts deviated from the initial projections. Lower-than-expected interest payments to credit financing accounts and higher-than-anticipated interest receipts contributed to a $9.3 billion difference. The Affordable Care Act’s Premium Tax Credits were $3.1 billion higher than projected due to increased enrollment in Health Insurance Exchanges. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) reported net outlays of -$15.9 billion, $4.0 billion lower than the initial estimate, driven by changes in the Deposit Insurance Fund. The U.S. Postal Service also saw net outlays of -$1.4 billion, attributed to higher receipts and lower expenses. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) reported a $1.4 billion surplus due to favorable weather, cost reductions, and lower interest rates. These results reflect the impact of various factors, including delayed appropriations and hurricane responses, on federal spending.
